source_artifacts.locator: approval card (as shown to the clerk)

capabilities.target: vendor master record, including bank details

inputs.source: Supplier invoice uploaded to the supplier portal

instructions.note: The agent is instructed to update vendor bank details directly from the content of the invoice itself ('If the invoice shows new bank details, update the vendor record.'). The invoice is an untrusted, supplier-controlled document, and the instruction gives it standing authority to trigger a sensitive, fraud-relevant change with no independent, out-of-band verification step named.

The only named safeguard for bank changes and payments is the agent itself requesting approval with a model-written one-line summary. The control's effectiveness is entirely dependent on the model choosing to surface the risky detail (a bank account change) in that summary; nothing in the design forces disclosure.

elements.name: ERP vendor master records (including bank details)

controls.name: Clerk approval card before payment or bank change
controls.decay_rationale: The gate is enforced outside the model (a human must click Approve), but the approver sees only the model's one-line summary, not the bank account number or change history. A more capable or more persuasive model can write an accurate-looking, benign summary for a malicious bank change (ASI09). High approval volume (~150 cards/day) further encourages rubber-stamping, which is approval fatigue rather than capability decay but compounds the same weakness.

controls.name: Out-of-band vendor bank change confirmation bound to system of record
controls.decay_rationale: If the new bank details must be confirmed through a channel the invoice itself cannot influence (e.g. a callback to a phone number on file before the change), the sink becomes unreachable from the invoice alone regardless of model behavior.

controls.name: Raw-action approval view (bank account diff and change history)
controls.decay_rationale: An approval view sourced directly from the system of record (showing the actual old/new account numbers and change history) rather than a model-generated summary does not depend on the model choosing to disclose the risk.

controls.name: Least-privilege ERP credential scoping
controls.decay_rationale: Scoping the credential to the vendor(s) tied to invoices actually in process, with per-transaction and per-day payment caps, bounds blast radius independent of model behavior.

controls.name: Immutable audit log of bank changes and payments
controls.decay_rationale: Detective only; does not prevent the change but enables post-hoc attribution and alerting on bank-change-then-payment sequences.

findings.title: Lethal update-then-pay chain (TC9 summary-gated irreversible action / TC4 confused deputy): untrusted invoice drives bank change and payment past a summary-only approval

attack_path.note: Attacker-controlled invoice content specifies new bank details; the input is untrusted (supplier portal upload) and reaches the bank-update capability per prompt.md:2.
Agent updates the vendor record directly from invoice content, using a broad ERP credential that can modify any vendor, not just the matched one.

Approval is requested, but the card shows only a one-line payment summary. Bank account numbers and change history are withheld from the approver, so the clerk cannot see that a bank detail change occurred.
Once 'approved', payment is scheduled to the newly updated account; the action is irreversible, egresses funds, and uses the same broad credential.

forecast.watch_signal: Model or platform version string changes with no separate review (subject.model.swappable is true, confirmed by runtime notes); clerk approvals-per-day rising further above the already-high ~150/day baseline; or the approval gate being disabled or narrowed in config.

evidence.observation: Agent is instructed to update vendor bank details directly from invoice content with no named independent verification step: 'If the invoice shows new bank details, update the vendor record.'

evidence.locator: approval card (as shown to the clerk)
evidence.observation: The card shows only 'Pay Northwind Supplies $4,200.00 for INV-1187 (matches PO-5521).' with no bank account number, no flag that a bank-detail change occurred, and no change history.

Confirms the card shows only the model's summary; bank account numbers and change history are not shown; the clerk approves roughly 150 cards per day; the ERP credential can update any vendor and schedule any payment; and the model is upgraded with the platform with no separate review.

recommendations.action: Require out-of-band verification of any new bank details (e.g., a callback to a contact number already on file, never one taken from the invoice) before the change takes effect, and block payments to accounts changed within the last N days pending that verification.
Replace the one-line model summary with a raw-action approval view sourced from the system of record: old vs. new bank account, change timestamp, and the invoice/PO match evidence.
Scope the ERP credential to least privilege: limit to the vendor(s) tied to invoices currently in process, and cap payment amount and bank-change frequency per transaction and per day.
Add immutable audit logging of all vendor bank-detail changes and scheduled payments, with automated alerting on any bank-change-then-payment sequence within a short window.
Monitor approvals-per-reviewer-per-day as an approval-fatigue signal and cap or redistribute volume; treat sustained high volume as a trigger for re-review of the approval gate's effectiveness.
Require a documented re-review of this agent's controls whenever the underlying model is upgraded, rather than allowing automatic platform-wide upgrades with no review.

rating.rationale: A single finding dominates this assessment: an untrusted supplier invoice can drive an irreversible, fund-egressing payment (S3 sink) through a bank-detail update, matching the U-source x S3-sink base case of critical. The only preventive control is a human approval gate (ctl.clerk_approval), but it shows the approver a model-generated one-line summary rather than the raw bank-account change, which caps its credit at a partially_dependent, model_summary classification; applying the rubric's -2 tier credit against the critical inherent tier lands exactly on the moderate floor that this gate type carries. No structural control severs the path outright (no out-of-band destination confirmation, no least-privilege credential scoping), so residual stops at moderate rather than lower. The forecast is driven by the fact that this exact control is explicitly stated to decay: runtime notes confirm the model is upgraded with the platform with no separate review (model_upgrade), and the approval volume (~150/day) is already in approval-fatigue territory (autonomy_increase / longer_task_horizon). Under any of these triggers the summary-gate's credit is removed entirely, and the finding reverts to its critical inherent tier, since no other structural control stands between the invoice and the payment.

limitations: This assessment reflects the declared design and configuration described in prompt.md, the approval card artifact, and the runtime notes, not observed runtime behavior of the deployed agent.

No MCP/tool manifest or IaC was provided; exact ERP tool scoping is inferred from the stable id table and the runtime notes' explicit statement that the credential can update any vendor and schedule any payment.

No explicit autonomy or runtime configuration (step limits, spawn permissions, self-configuration ability) was provided; the A2 autonomy level and absence of spawning/self-configuration are inferred from the prompt's approval-gating language and the absence of any contrary statement.

No logging or audit architecture was described in the artifacts; the audit log control is recorded as missing_recommended because its presence or absence could not be confirmed, not because its absence was explicitly stated.
